Abstract Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) after treatment with docetaxel and androgen receptor signaling inhibitors (ARSIs) has limited treatment options. Although enzalutamide has shown activity after abiraterone and docetaxel, robust evidence from randomized phase III trials is lacking. Deutenzalutamide, a novel derivative with slower metabolism and improved pharmacokinetics, may offer enhanced safety and efficacy. This phase III, double-blind trial conducted at 36 centers in China enrolled patients whose disease progressed on or who were intolerant to abiraterone and docetaxel, or who were ineligible for docetaxel. Patients were randomized (2:1) to receive deutenzalutamide 80 mg once daily or placebo until progression or unacceptable toxicity; the primary endpoint was radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS). Of 417 patients (276 deutenzalutamide; 141 placebo), all had previously received abiraterone, and 68% had also received docetaxel. Deutenzalutamide significantly improved rPFS (HR, 0.58; P = 0.0001), reducing the risk of progression by 42%. Although the initial OS analysis was not significant (HR, 0.95), sensitivity analyses adjusting for subsequent therapies showed significant OS benefits (HR, 0.65–0.73). Treatment-related grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 22.3% of patients treated with deutenzalutamide, compared with 15.0% with placebo. The most common treatment-related adverse event was anemia, reported at any grade in 21.2% versus 17.9%, with grade 3/4 anemia in 6.6% versus 2.9%, respectively. Notably, no seizures or falls were reported. In summary, deutenzalutamide significantly prolonged rPFS and, after adjustment, showed a potential OS benefit with a favorable safety profile, supporting its promise as a new treatment option for mCRPC. Introduction Prostate cancer remains a significant health concern and one of the leading causes of cancer-related mortality among men worldwide. 1 The burden of disease is increasing in parallel with population aging and changing risk profiles, and current projections indicate a substantial rise in both incidence and deaths in coming decades. Globally, new prostate cancer cases are expected to double from approximately 1.4 million per year in 2020 to 2.9 million per year in 2040, while mortality is projected to increase by 85% over the same period, from 375,000 deaths in 2020 to nearly 700,000 in 2040. 2 These trends emphasize the importance of improving systemic therapies for advanced disease, where survival remains limited and quality of life is frequently compromised by both tumor-related symptoms and cumulative treatment toxicity. Prostate cancer is also characterized by marked clinical heterogeneity, with interpatient and intratumoral differences in genomic and molecular alterations that shape the natural history of the disease and influence treatment responses. 3 Despite this complexity, androgen receptor (AR) signaling remains a central driver of prostate cancer initiation and progression. AR activity promotes tumor cell growth and survival across disease stages, and persistent androgen signaling is commonly observed even after castration-level testosterone has been achieved with androgen deprivation therapy (ADT). 4 Accordingly, inhibition of androgen signaling continues to represent a key therapeutic principle in localized, metastatic hormone-sensitive, and metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. The treatment landscape for mCRPC has evolved substantially over the past decade. The introduction and widespread adoption of ARSIs, including enzalutamide and abiraterone acetate, have improved clinically meaningful outcomes such as disease control and survival, and these agents are now integral components of standard care. 5 However, mCRPC remains a lethal condition, and most patients eventually develop progressive disease following exposure to one or more lines of therapy. In particular, a clinically challenging subgroup comprises patients whose disease progresses after both docetaxel chemotherapy and ARSI treatment. These patients frequently have limited remaining options due to tumor resistance, declining performance status, prior toxicities, and the reduced likelihood of response to further AR pathway suppression using similar approaches. From a practical standpoint, this setting represents an important unmet medical need in China, where there is currently no approved therapy specifically indicated for mCRPC after progression on docetaxel and an ARSI. Although several studies have suggested that enzalutamide may retain some activity in patients with mCRPC previously treated with docetaxel and abiraterone, 6 the magnitude and durability of benefit have been variable, and interpretation is constrained by the lack of randomized, well-designed trials in this specific post-docetaxel/post-ARSI context. Therefore, there is a clear need for new therapies that can effectively target AR signaling while addressing treatment resistance and tolerability challenges in heavily pretreated patients. Deutenzalutamide, a deuterated form of enzalutamide, has emerged as a potential option for patients with mCRPC who have exhausted standard therapies. Deuteration may confer pharmacokinetic advantages by slowing metabolism, increasing systemic exposure, and potentially enabling comparable pharmacodynamic activity at lower doses, which could translate into improved tolerability. 7 – 9 In addition, reducing central nervous system (CNS) exposure is of particular interest because CNS-related adverse effects have been clinically relevant with AR antagonists, especially in older patients and in those receiving multiple concomitant medications. Notably, deutenzalutamide demonstrates lower brain exposure than enzalutamide at similar plasma exposure levels, potentially alleviating CNS effects while maintaining peripheral antitumor activity. 7 Early clinical results have supported further development: in phase I trials, deutenzalutamide administered at 80 mg daily showed an 83.3% PSA 50 response rate with manageable safety in patients with mCRPC. 7 Beyond efficacy and safety signals, drug–drug interactions are an important consideration in this population due to frequent comorbidities and polypharmacy. Compared with enzalutamide, deutenzalutamide has fewer drug–drug interactions, with no dosage modifications required when coadministered with strong CYP2C8 inhibitors or CYP3A4 inducers (unpublished). Taken together, these features provide a mechanistic and clinical rationale to evaluate deutenzalutamide as a novel AR antagonist that may offer an improved benefit–risk profile for patients with mCRPC after docetaxel and ARSI therapy. Therefore, we conducted a phase III randomized trial to evaluate the efficacy and safety of deutenzalutamide in patients with mCRPC whose disease progressed after docetaxel and abiraterone. The results are intended to inform treatment strategies for this heavily pretreated population, particularly in China where therapeutic options remain limited. Results Patient characteristics Of the 538 patients screened, 417 were randomly assigned to receive either deutenzalutamide (276 patients) or placebo (141 patients) between March 2019 and December 2021 across 36 sites in China. Three patients withdrew, leaving 414 participants for analysis (274 in the deutenzalutamide group and 140 in the placebo group). All but three patients received their assigned treatment, leading to a safety population of 276 patients in the deutenzalutamide group and 141 in the placebo group (Fig. 1 ). Baseline characteristics were well matched between the two groups. All patients had received prior treatment with abiraterone, and the majority had previously received docetaxel (68.8% in the deutenzalutamide group vs 68.1% in the placebo group) (Table 1 ). measures The primary endpoint was analyzed after 218 rPFS events (135 in the deutenzalutamide arm and 83 in the placebo arm) had occurred. rPFS assessed by the investigator was statistically significantly prolonged in the deutenzalutamide arm compared to the placebo arm (HR, 0.58 [95% CI, 0.44–0.77]; P = 0.0001) (Fig. 2a ). The median rPFS was 5.55 months (95% CI, 4.83–7.36) in the deutenzalutamide arm and 3.71 months (95% CI, 2.86–5.49) in the placebo arm. The rPFS rates at 6, 12, and 24 months were 47% (95%, CI 39.2–53.8), 29% (95% CI, 21.7–36.7), and 18% (95% CI, 10.7–26.4) in the deutenzalutamide arm versus 33% (95% CI, 23.6–43.3) and 6% (95% CI, 0.7–19.6), and - (95% CI - to -) in the placebo arm, respectively. The efficacy of deutenzalutamide was maintained in sensitivity analyses, with an HR = 0.60 and 0.67 and P = 0.0002 and 0.0012 (Supplementary Table 3 ). These analyses included censoring subjects who used other antitumor treatments before progression or death on the day before and treated such subjects as events without censoring for rPFS calculation. HRs for rPFS favored deutenzalutamide across all prespecified subgroups (Fig. 3 ). rPFS by BICR also demonstrated a similar trend in the primary analyses (HR, 0.60 [95% CI, 0.45–0.81]; P = 0.0006, Fig. 2b ). Other secondary efficacy endpoints were consistent with these results (Supplementary Fig. 1 and 2 , and Supplementary Table 1 ). Preferred terms were coded using the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities version 23.0 Discussion The efficacy of deutenzalutamide in extending rPFS was significantly superior to that of placebo, as evidenced by the statistically significant improvement observed in this study. The HR for rPFS was 0.58 (95% CI, 0.44–0.77; P = 0.0001), indicating a 42% reduction in the risk of progression or death in the deutenzalutamide arm compared to the placebo arm. Although the median rPFS improvement with deutenzalutamide over placebo is modest (1.8 months), deutenzalutamide maintains a marked long-term rPFS advantage, with 29% vs 6% rPFS at 12 months and 18% vs none at 24 months. The rPFS benefit was consistent across all prespecified subgroups, including age, presence of visceral metastases, and prior docetaxel treatment. Central imaging results aligned with local investigator findings, offering additional assurance of therapeutic efficacy. Exploratory OS analyses revealed promising outcomes with deutenzalutamide. While the final OS analysis at the time point did not reach statistical significance, sensitivity analyses adjusting for subsequent antitumor therapies demonstrated a survival benefit with deutenzalutamide over placebo (HR ~ 0.65–0.73). These findings highlight that deutenzalutamide can offer a viable treatment option for patients with mCRPC who have not responded to prior therapies, particularly when considering the confounding effects of subsequent treatments on OS. The management of mCRPC, particularly in the context of sequential use of ARSIs such as abiraterone following enzalutamide or vice versa, is complicated by cross-resistance due to their action on the same signaling pathway. While the overall clinical benefits are often limited, some patients experience long-term advantages. 6 Our study is the first to demonstrate the efficacy of deutenzalutamide in improving rPFS and showing a positive OS trend in a well-designed, double-blind pivotal trial, with similar efficacy observed in patients regardless of prior docetaxel treatment (Fig. 3 ). There is an unmet medical need for mCRPC patients post-ARSI and chemotherapy, particularly in China, where abiraterone and docetaxel are widely used. 10 , 11 Initial investigations suggest that enzalutamide offers clinical benefits for patients unresponsive to abiraterone/docetaxel. 6 , 12 Our research confirms the efficacy of deutenzalutamide in this setting, reinforcing its potential as a viable treatment option. Cabazitaxel, approved for mCRPC after docetaxel treatment, may present as an alternative treatment in this setting (CARD study). 13 Despite its longer median rPFS (8.0 months) compared to deutenzalutamide (5.6 months), deutenzalutamide offers a substantially better long-term rPFS rate at 24 months (18.8% vs. ~5%). Additionally, while the median OS is comparable between the two treatments, deutenzalutamide shows a notably higher long-term OS rate (~30% vs <2% at 30 months). However, cabazitaxel’s association with increased risks of neutropenia, infections, and gastrointestinal toxicities remains a significant concern. Recent developments in Lu-177 PSMA therapy provide another treatment avenue for mCRPC patients with PSMA-positive disease by delivering targeted radiation to PSMA-expressing tumor cells. 14 Despite its promise, the limited availability and specialized requirements pose challenges for widespread adoption. Deutenzalutamide, a deuterated variant of enzalutamide, shows promise in addressing CNS-related safety issues associated with enzalutamide and other AR inhibition therapies in mCRPC. By modifying the pharmacokinetic profile of enzalutamide, deutenzalutamide reduces brain exposure to the active drug, potentially decreasing the incidence of CNS-related adverse effects 7 . Our comparative analysis between deutenzalutamide and historical data from the pivotal AFFIRM trial of enzalutamide reveals a significant improvement in the CNS-related safety profile of deutenzalutamide (Supplementary Table 2 ). 15 , 16 Specifically, deutenzalutamide demonstrated lower frequencies of fatigue, dizziness, and abnormal sensations. Notably, no cases of epilepsy, falls, or anxiety were observed in patients treated with deutenzalutamide. Additionally, the occurrence of grade 3 fatigue was significantly reduced with deutenzalutamide (3.3%) compared to enzalutamide (9%). It is important to acknowledge the limitations of comparing data from different trials. However, the present study showed that deutenzalutamide exhibited a favorable safety profile, with adverse events consistent with those common in the mCRPC patient population. This study has several limitations to consider when interpreting the results. First, there was no active comparator (e.g., cabazitaxel, enzalutamide, or Lu-PSMA-617), which was not approved in China at the time of study design. Although the median rPFS with deutenzalutamide was similar to that reported for enzalutamide in post abiraterone mCRPC (5.55 months in this study vs. 5.7 months in TRANSFORMER and 5.55 months in PSMAfore), 17 , 18 deutenzalutamide appears to offer a substantially better long-term rPFS than enzalutamide. This suggests a potential advantage for deutenzalutamide, particularly since TRANSFORMER and PSMAfore enrolled only patients who progressed on abiraterone, whereas our cohort included patients who had progressed on both abiraterone and docetaxel. Second, adjustment of OS based on subsequent therapies was not predefined in the protocol. Given the absence of a standard therapy for this population in China at the start of the study, crossover was not an option. To fully understand the main factors contributing to the OS results, in addition to the previously described IPCW and RPSFTM analyses, comprehensive sensitivity analyses were conducted using common methods on OS analyses, including accelerated failure time (AFT) models, stratified proportional hazards models, two-stage estimation, and analyses excluding patients receiving subsequent antitumor therapies. All analyses largely converged on the conclusion that OS benefits persisted after adjustment for subsequent therapies. While these sensitivity analyses were not prespecified, they provided valuable insights into the treatment effect on OS. Third, this study does not specify the treatments patients received during the mHSPC phase. It is plausible that many participants underwent androgen deprivation therapy, with abiraterone and docetaxel introduced upon progression to mCRPC. Explicit documentation of prior therapeutic regimens and disease context would enhance the interpretability and generalizability of the findings. Future work should routinely report prior therapeutic regimens and disease context to better contextualize AR-targeted responses. Additionally, patients were not prescreened for AR mutations and tumor burden. In late-stage mCRPC patients, resistance often involves AR mutations and/or tumor burden. A recent study indicated that patients with circulating AR alterations may not benefit from continuing enzalutamide. 19 Future work should integrate prospective molecular and clinical stratification to define subgroups most likely to benefit from AR-targeted therapy. Given the observed 24-month rPFS benefit in a subset of long responders, incorporating biomarker-driven selection (e.g., AR mutational status, AR signaling activity and tumor burden) could sharpen patient enrichment, personalize treatment and enhance the translational impact of AR-targeted strategies in this setting. In conclusion, deutenzalutamide, a novel AR antagonist with an enhanced safety profile and reduced drug‒drug interaction effects, has been validated as a viable treatment for mCRPC patients who have shown resistance to abiraterone and docetaxel therapies. These results highlight its potential as a valuable addition to the AR-targeted therapy arsenal, particularly in settings where post abiraterone/docetaxel options remain limited. Methods and materials Study design and participants The HC-1119-04 study was a randomized, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase III clinical trial in patients who had previously been treated with abiraterone and docetaxel. Eligible patients had a histologically or cytologically confirmed diagnosis of prostate adenocarcinoma without small cell features, castration-level testosterone (<50 ng/dL or 1.73 nmol/L), prior treatment with abiraterone and docetaxel or intolerance to these therapies, metastasis confirmed by bone scan or CT/MRI, and progressive disease defined according to Prostate Cancer Working Group 3 (PCWG3) criteria including at least two rising PSA values or radiographic progression with or without a PSA rise. 20 Key exclusion criteria included brain metastasis and a history of seizures or a predisposition to seizures. The study was designed by the sponsor, Hinova Pharmaceuticals Inc., in collaboration with a steering committee of independent investigators. The trial met regulatory requirements and has received approval from the lead institution, the Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center (No: 1901196-12) and the ethics committees of each participating center. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and the Good Clinical Practice Guidelines of the International Conference on Harmonization (ICH). 21 Placebo control was ethically approved in China due to a lack of standard-of-care options post abiraterone/docetaxel at trial initiation. Regulatory guidelines permitted placebo in this context (Chinese NMPA, 2019). All patients provided written informed consent. An external independent data monitoring committee reviewed the safety and efficacy data. All authors were involved in the writing or critical review and editing of the manuscript and attest to the integrity of the trial and the accuracy and completeness of the data reported. Randomization Eligible patients were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio using an independent randomization system to receive either deutenzalutamide or placebo, minimizing the number of patients on placebo. Randomization was stratified by visceral metastases and prior docetaxel treatment. Baseline imbalances in age and performance status were statistically adjusted via Cox regression. A contract research organization (CRO) generated and securely stored the randomization list until database lock. The treatment assignment remained masked for patients, sponsor staff, and physicians, with both active and placebo kits packaged identically to ensure blinding. Crossover to deutenzalutamide was not permitted post progression. Endpoints The primary endpoint was rPFS assessed by the investigator, defined as the time from randomization to death from any cause or the first objective evidence of radiographic disease progression, either in soft-tissue disease per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors, version 1.1 (RECIST 1.1) 22 or in bone per PCWG3 guidelines. The key secondary endpoint was OS. Other secondary endpoints included rPFS assessed by blinded independent central review (BICR), disease control rate (DCR), duration of response, objective response rate (ORR), PSA response rate, time to PSA progression (TTPP), and safety. Patients received either placebo or deutenzalutamide at a dose of 80 mg orally once daily (two 40 mg capsules) for 28-day cycles, with dose reductions to 40 mg permitted for toxicity. Efficacy assessments included soft-tissue imaging by CT/MRI and bone imaging by radionuclide bone scan, survival status, and PSA levels. Tumor assessments were performed by CT/MRI at week 8 (Day 1 of Cycle 2), week 16 (Cycle 3), and every 2 cycles thereafter and bone scan on Day 1 of Cycle 4 and every 3 cycles thereafter. Abnormal bone lesions were confirmed with CT scan with bone windows or MRI. Safety assessments occurred twice in cycle 1, once in each subsequent cycle, and until 30 days after the last study drug dose. Statistical analysis The efficacy analysis included all randomized patients; the safety analysis included all randomized patients who had received at least one dose of study drug. For the primary efficacy endpoint rPFS, a sample of 417 patients in a 2:1 ratio for deutenzalutamide and placebo with 213 rPFS events would provide the trial with 90% power to detect an HR of 0.667 with a two-sided alpha of 0.025. The prespecified final OS analysis was planned after approximately 319 OS events, which would provide approximately 90% power to detect an HR of 0.72 with a two-sided alpha level of 0.025. A hierarchical hypothesis testing approach was used: rPFS, then OS. Hypothesis testing of rPFS and OS was performed using the p values generated from the stratified log-rank test. The HR and 95% confidence interval (CI) for the difference between treatment groups in rPFS and OS were estimated using the stratified Cox regression model, including treatment as the explanatory variable. Medians and corresponding 95% CIs were estimated by the Kaplan‒Meier method. Other efficacy endpoints were not part of the study hypothesis testing, and the results are reported as point estimates and 95% CIs without multiplicity adjustment. In both treatment groups, post progression anti-neoplastic therapies other than the investigational drug were commonly used, which could significantly impact OS. Therefore, sensitivity analyses on OS using IPCW and RPSFT were also performed to adjust for the effects of subsequent therapies. 23 – 25 All statistical analyses were performed using SAS software, version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC).
